claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are predominantly governed by lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch.
Local strain fields produced by atomic-size mismatch impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances yield strength.
Reducing atomic-size disparity should proportionally decrease hardness and strength.
Annealed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can serve as a homogenized, single-phase FCC baseline.
Partially replacing Mn with an element closer in atomic size to Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni will reduce the alloy's overall lattice distortion.
Atomic-size mismatch induces lattice distortions and associated local strain fields.
Greater lattice distortion raises the energy barrier for dislocation propagation during plastic deformation.
Reducing lattice distortion lowers resistance to dislocation motion.
The baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy will have greater lattice distortion than the modified alloy.
The baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy will exhibit higher Vickers hardness than the modified alloy.
The baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy will exhibit higher yield strength than the modified alloy.
Lattice distortion is a dominant strengthening mechanism in uniform equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed relationship applies to single-phase, equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys dominated by solid-solution strengthening.
The proposed relationship should hold at ambient and moderately elevated temperatures when significant diffusion and phase transformations are absent.
X-ray diffraction line broadening and high-resolution TEM strain mapping can be used to characterize the proposed lattice distortion.
Failure of the reduced-size-mismatch alloy to show a statistically significant reduction in both hardness and yield strength would reject lattice distortion as the primary contributor.
